# How this specification was produced

**This describes software that already exists.** It was not written from a brief, a plan or an intention: it was written by reading online-shopping-system-advanced, on branch `master`.

That changes how to read everything that follows. An interface described here is one that is live now, not one somebody proposes. A data model here has rows in it. A gap here is not a decision waiting to be made — it is something about a running system that nobody could currently tell you.

## What was read

| | |
|---|---|
| Repository | `online-shopping-system-advanced` |
| Branch | `master` |
| Files read in full | 6 |
| Files in the repository | 394 |

Files are chosen for what they describe — manifests, entry points, routes, schema, migrations, tests, pipelines and documentation. Dependencies, build output, lock files and binaries are never read: a lock file proves a dependency exists, while the manifest beside it says what the dependency is *for*, and only the second describes a system.

If that coverage looks thin against what you know is in there, treat the sections below as a starting point rather than a survey.

## What the code shows, and this specification must describe

Each of these is visible in the repository. They are work for whoever finishes this document, not open questions.

### Write down the data model and what owns it

The code reaches MySQL. The specification needs the entities, their relationships and their retention rules — the parts a schema shows the shape of but never the reason for.

Seen in: `README.md`, `admin/admin/index.php`, `admin/server/server.php`

### List the external services this depends on

The code talks to Google Cloud. Every one of those is an outage you do not control, and the specification is where the behaviour when it is down gets decided.

Seen in: `README.md`

## What the code could not answer

Each of these is an *absence*, and an absence is not proof. Tests may live in another repository; a pipeline may be configured outside the code. The value of listing them is that this is the one moment when asking is cheap — once the specification is signed, every one of them becomes an assumption somebody made silently.

### No automated tests were found

Nothing matching a test path or filename turned up. If they live in another repository, say so in the specification; if they do not exist, the acceptance criteria are the only description of correct behaviour this system will have.

### No build or release pipeline was found

No workflow, pipeline or Jenkins file. How this gets from a commit to running software is then knowledge somebody holds rather than something the repository states.

### Almost nothing is written down

One documentation file or fewer. That is the usual reason for generating a specification from code, and it also means this profile had little prose to work from — read the suggestions below with that in mind.

### No container or infrastructure definition was found

Nothing describes where this runs. The specification will have to state the runtime, the dependencies and the configuration from somebody's memory, which is the version that goes stale first.

## What no amount of reading can produce

Code shows what a system does. It never shows what it is *for*, what was promised to whom, what it must not do, or what happens when a dependency is down. Those sections of this specification cannot be recovered from a repository and have to be written by somebody who knows — which is the argument for doing it now, while the people who know are still here.
